newsitem.title: UK: British employers condemn ruling on work hours.
newsitem.headline: British employers condemn ruling on work hours.

text.p: Britain's employers united on Tuesday in condemnation of the European Court of Justice's refusal to exempt Britain from rules limiting working hours.

At the Confederation of British Industry's (CBI's) annual conference here, CBI director general Adair Turner attacked the European Union's Working Time Directive, which limits the working week to 48 hours, as "legislation at its worst: detailed, prescriptive regulations followed by extensive caveats and exemptions."
Smaller companies were seen as the biggest vitims of the ruling. The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said nearly half of the country's small businesses employ people for more than 48 hours a week.

Andrew Buxton, chairman of banking group Barclays Plc, said "Big companies will find it relatively easy to cope with this. It is certainly not over-concerning for Barclays. It's the small companies that will find this yet another piece of red tape."
But there was also concern that the ruling would further worsen Britain's tattered relations with the EU.

Prime Minister John Major signalled on Monday night that the government would not take the European Court's ruling lying down, pledging to use Britain's veto to scupper progress at the Inter Governmental Conference (IGC) unless it got its way on working hours.

Mario Monti, the EU internal market commissioner participating in a CBI debate on Europe on Tuesday morning, said "I hope every member state including the UK would see the big disadvantages...of not taking a cooperative and active stance in negotiations."

But Monti and business leaders all pointed to loopholes in the directive as a way out for Britain, which views its flexible working practices as a major lure for foreign investors and a key factor in its relative success at creating jobs.

Barclays' Buxton, who heads the CBI's economic affairs committee, commented that "Europe has not created one job in the past five years, the UK certainly has. One of the reasons Britain has attracted all this inward investment is its freer labour market."
The CBI immediately suggested a raft of ways for the government to get round the court ruling, including allowing the 48-hour week to be averaged over periods of six or even 12 months.
It suggested that legislation could also be introduced to allow individual employees to work more than 48 hours a week if they wished.
The timing of the European Court ruling, on the last day of the CBI's conference, underlined British industry's love-hate relationship with the EU.

While businessmen are adamant about keeping Britain's perceived advantages over competitors, particularly in terms of labour market flexibility and opting out of the Social Chapter, there is clear exasperation with the increasingy Euro-sceptical line followed by the government.
British Chamber of Commerce president David Richardson told the conference that politicians "should stop playing games with our future in Europe."

"The business view is that we are in, we are right to be in and that we should stay in. What business needs is a government which is committed to Europe (and) is influential in the key decisions that affect Europe," Richardson added.
